The riots which took place in the earlv part ol June in Silesia tiave been to, lowed t'v others in Prague ; and commissions aie sitting in both districts to explote the u-al causes ol these excesses. Fiom the various accounts from those districts these cause are pietiy plainly excessive lowness ol the price of labour, and, to a great extent, utter want of work. For a long period the distress among the hand loom linen weavers has been dreadful. This has now extended itself to the cotton spinners, and the description of the appearance ot these þÿworkpeople Ihe formerly simple, peaceful, and industrious, ami happy inhabitants of the Silesian valleys, is heartrending. Before Christmas some disturbances took place þÿ the distress has gone on increasing On the one hand the formidable competition of England ; on the other, the strict closing of the trade actoss the frontiers with Russia, has brought the people to desperation. They atirihuted all their miseries to the introduction of machinery, and accordingly against that they turn ed their fury. Collecting in a mass of more than 1000, they marched w ith a white curtain torn down from a window, and hoisted on a pole as a banner, and to the singing of a song which had long been sung through all the district to express their injuries, into the populous manufacturing villages of Peters waldau and Langenbielau. where they attacked the chief factories. Attempts weie made

to turn away their fury bv the distribution of money, but, in most cases, in vain. Windows, roof's, machinery, furniture, all met with one common destruction. The stores of yarn, indigo, mannfacturedgoods, spindles, &o , were all carried out and tfung into the millstreams. During 24 hours that it required to get an order from Breslau for the employment of military, this work of demolition and plunder went on. The soldiers, on their arrival, fired on the mob, and killed 13 on the spot, besides wounding many others. The rioters then fled to the hills and woods, whence the soldiers hunted them out. Upwards of a hundred were conveyed to the prison at Schweidniz. The Prince Adalbert of Prussia hastened to Breslau to ascertain the real facts of the case. There, also, the mob manifested a disposition to the same excesses; broke the street lamps, and the windows of the houses, and of the Reformed Church. No sooner did die news arrive in Prague than the cotton spinners also assembled on the I7di and 18ih of June, and demolished the machinery ot the factories, to which they attributed the lowness of their wages and their consequent miseries. All these excesses, except those at Peterwaldau, have been attended Without loss ol file. Thus Germany is beginning to taste some of the sours as well as the sweets of the manufacturing s\ stem,

WAtl as it is. þÿ History, which is but too much a record of violence and fraud, presents war to us in its most attractive aspect ; garnished with triumph and tinsel and glorv ; war as seen only in its grand results of conquest and acquisition. Hut to know what war realiy is. we must go into its þÿdetails look not at grand armies, but at regiments, companies and individuals, and see how the iron hand ot Moloch deals with them. For instance, here is an episode of General Naþÿpier s þÿ þÿglorious campaign in Scinde. from the United Service Gazette. The following interesting narrative lias been furnished to us from India by an of beer of this distinguished regiment: þÿ About the latter end of August, lc42, the 28th regiment, nearly 800 strong, arrived and landed at Bombay, in high health, and spirits, from New South Wales; ard rarlv in the following month orders were received for its immediate embarkation for field service in Scinde, The regiment accoidinglv proceeded from Bombay to Kuratchee in the steamcis Scmiramis, Zenobia and Berenice. On this passage of four da) s onlv, between sixty and seventy men of the 2Hih died of cholera. The major general, shortly after fiis arrival at Kuratchee, proceeded up the Indus to Suekker, and there fixed his head quarters, i he 28th remained in camp, first at Mnnora þÿ1 oint. and afterward near Kuratchee, and lost, by death, of Scinde fever and cholera, one lieutenant colonel, one captain and two lieutenants, besides a large number of men.

About the middle of February following the Scinde war broke out. No intelligence of or trom the major general having for a considerable time been received at Kuratchee and the Scindians in the vicinity having exhibited a hostile feeling toward the British troops there, by cutting oil supplies, &o , the commandant, without waiting lor instructions resolved to occupy the lort und town of Kuratchee. The British flag was hoisted, the Killcdar was taken prisoner, and all public property was seized. The property subsequently thrown into the general ptize fund. The whole country was in arms, supplies and communications were cut off, and the troops at Kuratchee were continually on salt provisions. '1 he camp, if the expression may be used, was in a stale of siege. The 28th were busily employ ed in entrenching their camp, which was sui rounded by strong oui-iving picqueis of the regiment. An attack upon the camp was daily, even hourly, expected. Toward the end of April, .Shere Mahomed, the only Bcllnochec chief of note at largere-assembled a large force and threatened a second time to march upon Hyderabad. The captured treasure was in the fortress and the fielioochees calculated upon repossessing themselves ol it. No European regiment w'as there, and his Excellency's position was somewhat critical. A sudden order was received in consequence, at Kuratchee, for the nuncli ol the 28th, anrt early in May the regnneiit look the field, and moved toward Hyderabad. On the march his

quartermaster general Came into camp with information that the general only awaited the arrival of the regiment to recommence hostilities. The 28th inarched intr> the fort of Hyderabad on or about llic 12 ill of May. " 0

® r» ® si 'x z » y 3 s. 184.1, having, from the excessive heat lost on its march one lieutenant and a number of men. For three weeks the regiment remained in j garrison at llvdeiabad, suflering greatly from the climate and the fatigue of its march. The losses of the regiment here by fever were immense. The adjutant died, and the remains of three or four soldiers were every morning and evening consigned to the grave. The deaths were sudden ; and here it may not be amiss to record an cxtruoidinarv instance of sudden death which occurred. A pioneer of the regiment who was usually employed with others in digging graves, one evening dug a grave more than was required, in which the poor fellow was himself buried early on the following morning. About the beginning of June, Shere Mahommed who hud been informed of the sickly state of the European troops in garrison matched toward Hyderabad, and his Excellency resulted to move out and meet him. 'I he Ameer approached witli confidence. The sickly stale of the British troops, and the excessive heat of the season must he imagined, paralyse the general, and prevent the Europeans fmm acting. His Excellency, notwithstanding these unfavorable circumstances, took the field, and those of the 28th regiment, w ho were able to move, Jolt the fort. Not above 250 men ol the corps could be found capable of bearing arms, and they were in a most weakly state. The army, however, assembled at a village about sixteen miles from Hyderabad, and on the 15th ot June firing was heard. The

general ordered the troops to prepare to march. The 28th fell in, and his Excellency addressed them. In their anxiety to match, men who were worn out with disease had turned out, and, poor fellows, they could not march. þÿ Ere the column had moved a mite or two numbers fell The heat was insup portable þÿ thermometer ISO in tents The road was literally coveted with soldiers in a state of exhaustion, and this match ol onlv three þÿdays continuance deprived the regiment of one lieutenant and upward of forty men, who died of apoplexy. The Belochees dispersed, and Shere Mahomed fled to the desert. Thus the war ended, and Scinde was annexed, as a province, to the British territory. The 28th, with a battalion of natives, formed the garrison of Hyderabad until the !2th of October last, when the 2Sih, with the captured or prize property, were embarked on the Indus, and proceeded to the mouth ot the river. There the booty, about £000.000, was transhipped for Bombay, and the regiment for Kuratchee. On the arrival of the 28th at Kuratchee, the number of men on parade, including officers, was fifty four. The regiment was, in fact, almost annihilated and its remains were shortly afterward embarked for Bombay. Bv tliis service the 28th left dead in þÿS cinrle one lieutenant colonel, one major, one captain, the aojutant, and five other lieutenants, besides one lieutenant since dead of Scinde fever. One captain, three lieutenants, the surgeon and quarter master. who had suffered

and are suffering from Scinde fever, have left the regiment for the recovery of health, and þÿExcellency s others will doubtless have to quit India on the same account. The sergeant major, the assistant sergeant major, the orderly room clerk (sergeant), the paymaster's sergeant he þÿarmourer s sergeant, the schoolmaster's sergeant, twenty-nine sergeants, and about 250 i an it and file of the regiment also died in

Scinde, besides a pioporti< ftam number ol women and children. This took place within the period ol tbit icon months. Shortly after its arrival at Bombay, the regiment, whirl bad been there re enforced by 400 recruits from England, marched li>r Poona, wlieie it arrived on the 90: h of December last, having left at Bombay 250 !Scuide men witf, a number of officers, sick and unable to inarch. The greater pan of the s 'Idiorv, it is supposed, will never do another day's duty.

A Dreadful Steamboat Explosion. þÿ The Baltimore Patriot of Friday evening contains a letter, dated at llio de Janeiro on the 28'h May, giving an account of a steamboat accident which occurred at that place on the 25' It, attended with a gteat loss of life. The following is an extract : þÿ This city was thrown into great excitement on Saturday last try an oceui tence w Inch has clothed a large number of its inhabitants in mourning and created a gloom over the whole city. ( )n the opposite aide of the harbor and distant about four miles, is a village, which numbers about three thousand inhabitants, and where a number of the most respected inhabitants reside, as being more retired than in the bustle of Bio. Two small steamboats piy every hour during the day between the two places, so that the number of passengers is large, especially upon holydays, for recreation. Saturday was one of these days, and at four þÿo clock in the afternoon about three hundred persons entered from the wharf of the city, and the boat had just pushed from the moorings when tiie boiler burst with a most awful explosion. þÿ A friend of mine, w ho was present, represents the scene as the most heart rending that the heart can conceive. The boat was a complete wreck, and, amidst the shrieks of the wounded, the cries of the drowning, and the confusion of the moment, the most callous heart would have melted into tender nes«. The mutilated remains were gathered as soon as possible and removed to a neighboring hospital þÿ some

with the loss of a limb, some dreadfully scalded þÿ and upon numbering them it was found t ha t there were eightty six wounded in the house, besides those removed to ptivatc dwellings. There were fifty two ascertained to have been killed and several persons are missing yet. þÿ Seven or eight have died since, and I am informed there are as many as twenty who are pronounced incurable and will probably linger in agony tor several days. The number of wounded who are still living, as far ns ascertained, is sixty five. This is the first accident of the kind which has ever occurred here and has caused great excitement. Ai| places of public amusement were dosed and have not since been þÿopened.

Loan to hie West Inotes. þÿ An important arrangement is nearly concluded between the executive government and the West India interest for the relief of the latter under the increased competition to which they will be exposed by the passing of the new Sugar Hill. In order to enable the West India colonies to avail themselves of an increased quantity of labour, embracing immigration from India and China, with as little delay as possible, it is proposed that a pat bamentai y guarantee be given for a loan to he raised of a million and a half ster ling We believe the principle of the measure is already arranged, and all that remains to be settled applies to mere matters of detail. Added to this, as the crown of French civilization in Africa, you must listen to the singing gir Is of the musical soirees cl the cates. The position and internal arrangements ot the factory weie as follows : þÿ The barracoon is situated at the opposite side of the town, to give the owner an opportunity of secreting his slaves in an adjoining fmest in case ot surprise bv a man ol war. þÿ It is an enclosure of one acre or more, one si-'e of which is formed by a substantial bamboo house, perhaps 200 feet long, and 80 wide ; this is the sleeping apartment of t tie slaves. The appearance of these miserable beings, together with the hardships and privations which they sutler, tnav be inferred from that portion of the narrative which follows: þÿ Among the slaves were persons of both sexes, from f> to 40 years ot age. With the exception of some 20 or 30 invalids, all were seated on togs laid lengthwise and about three feet apart, under the open shade already mentioned. There was one company winch pai ticularly arrested my attention and atlecied my heart. It was made up of motheis who had recently been heieli of their children. When udants aie born in the barracoon, or when they are brought there with their mothers, because it is inconvenient to keep them in tiie factory, and almost impossible to carry them across the ocean, thev are subjected to a premature and violent death. 1 speak advisedly, when 1 alfirm that ibis is a common occur leuce in the operations of the slave uade; and it was iu tin- way, 1 was credibly mloimed, that these sorrowing females had been sundered flour their ollspiiug. Steam Power. þÿ A pint of water may be evaporated by two ounces of coals. In its evaporation it swells into 210 gallons of steam, with a mechanical force sufficient to raise a weight ot 37 tons, a foot high. The steam thus produced has a pressure equal to that of common atmospheric air ; and by allowing it to expand by vir tue of its elasticity, a further mechanical force may be obtained, at least equal in amount to the former. A pint of water, therefore, and two ounces of coals are thus rendered capable of doing as much work as is equivalent to 74 tons raised a foot high. The circumstances under whicti the steam engine is worked on a railway are not favourable to the economy of fuel. Nevertheless a pound ol coke hurtled in a locomotive engine will evapoiate about five pints of water. In their evaporation they will exert a mechanical force sulTxcient to draw two tons on the railway a distance of one mile in two minutes. Four horses Working in a stage coach on a common road are necessary to draw the same weight the same distance in six þÿminutes. Globe.

Respected Elders and Members of the REFORMED lJU'ICH CHURCH ' 'I lie interesting occasion which calls us together this day, is one well calculated to awaken the deepest emotions, and kindle the warmest gratitude of your heaits. Precisely one Century iias elapsed, since this congregation was first planted on these Western shores. And during that long period of one hundred revolving years, has the Almighty kindly watched over tiie interest of your beloved Zion. And after protecting her through many vicissitudes þÿ He! has now crowned his mercies, by permitting you this day to found anolhei house of Worship. Since the year 1744, from which this Church dates her origin þÿ at least three generations of her members have slept the sleep of death. Her early founders and their children have long ete this n ingled with their parent clay þÿ ashes to þÿashes and dust to dust ; but still w ith undiminished numbers and untarnished Glory lour Zion lives. Amid a thousand changing scenes, God hath spared her: though she hath suffered many sore þÿafflictions though her noble place ol woiship has been razed to the ground by t tie destructive þÿelements though for 17 years deprived of the sacred Ministry. Though called to witness seasons of fearful degeneracy ; our Zion still lives. Though severely tried in the furnace of affliction, she still lives in youthful vigour, and so far from þÿoverwhelming her trials have rather purified her and made her more zealous and devoted to the cause of God.

And now we trust that the dark days of our Zion are over, and that once again she will flourish in all her pristine glory, Alanv of your bathers (who have gone to rest) have desired to see this day þÿ but for you has this privilege been reserved to witness the foundation of this Holy Temple. burelv then, Oh! surelv, your hearts should burn with warmest love and gratitude to Almighty God, for this signal evidence of his Alerey toward you. And Oh! that you may ever show yourselves worthy of this favour, and that you mav evince your gratitude, not in words only, hut in every deed and truth! Alay the work which you have this day commenced long stand a mon ument of God's grace towards you: and of your thankfulness to him ! May it ever be to you, and to your childrens children the House of praise and the very gates of flea ven ! May it ever prove the safe Repository ol the truth, as it is in Jesus, and be the birthplace of a thousand immortal souls! May the father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the only wise and true Jehovah bless and prosper this work, which his servants have commenced in his Name. And now most Honored Governor permit mo in behalf of the Elders and members of this congregation, to return you many thanks for the favor you have done us. It is indeed

a glorious sign when our Rulers are willing to unite with us in advancing the Redeemer's cause. We hail the token with delight as the harbinger of better things. Long may you live sir! as a faithful servant to your Heavenly King as you always have been to vour earthly sovereign. And permit us to express through you, in the most respectful manner, our great obligations to bis Excellency Governor General von Scholten, lor the deep interest he has manifested in this work from its very commencement; assure our respected chief magistrate, that his disinterested kindness will be long temenibeied by the Reiormed Dutch Congregation. Permit me also to thank you Beloved broiher in Christ, and the congregation over which you preside, for the many lavors we have received at your hands For at least 15 years our churches have been united in the closest bonds of brotherly love þÿ Through that long space of time (as far as 1 am a w are nothing iias occurred to interrupt our harmony. Peace li as reigned over our mutual counsels, and christian love has never been sundered Under these circumstances, we separate from you with deep regret and nothing hut necessity lias compelled us to this course. But while we thus separate, we earnestly desire, that our mutual love and christian fellowship may never be disturbed. Though in some points of religious faith we may differ, vet in the great Essential; "Christ and him crucified" þÿ we agree with most perfect unanimity. Let our only strife then be, who shall love ttial fcaviour most and

serve him best. To you also fellow citizens, who have assisted us by your subscriptions, we return many thanks. Through your kind aid we have been enabled io proceed in our work; without it, our success would have been doubtful. We feci most happy that in this matter all religious bigotry has been laid aside, and that the children of Abraham have united wiili the followers of .other, with the churches of England and of Rome, to assist in the building of this Temple to the Long Long may that Gatholic Spirit of benevolence prevail, and far distant be the dnv, when envious bigotry shall prevail in its stead. And now my friends, last but chief of all our earthly benefactors, we would mention with profound respect the name of our beloved Sovereign King Christian VIM. Trie ft iend of religion, the defender of the Christian faith and the firm protector of liberty of conscience- þÿ he is worthy of our warmest admiration- þÿ Long may he live to reign over us- þÿ And long may we prove his most faithlul subjects.

The possibility of a mistake was readily surmised, and a few brief inquiries showed the party that they had been set down at the wrong then ire. Floweis of all kinds are in great request amongst the inhabitants, who employ them in the decoration of their dwelling houses and temples In going up the river towards the Fatee Garden, 1 met bouts in great numbers loaded vvttli the branches of peach and plum trees in bloom, enkiantbus quinquedora, camellias, cockscombSj magnolias, and various other things which flower at this season. Ihe enkiantbus is brought down from the hills with the buds just expanding; and after being placed in water for a day or two. the floweis come out as healthy and fresh as if the branches had not been removed from the parent tree. This plant is a great favourite amongst the Chinese. The common jonquil, too, comes in for a most extensive share of patronage ; and in the streets of Canton one meets with thousands of bulbs growing in small pans amongst water and a few white stones. In this the Chinese exhibit th< f peculiar propensity for dwarf and monstrous growth, by planting the bulbs upside down, and making the plants and flowers assume curious twisted forms, which are mast agreeable to the eyes ol a Chinaman Large quaniiliesof all these flowers are exposed tor sale in many ot the shops and in the corner! of tiie streets in Canton, where they seem to ha eagerly bought up by the Chiocae, who

tio.lar seas »n Not only are houses and temples decorated, hut the boats on the river also come iti (or a most extensive share. þÿ Some were so timid as to avoid us as if The (lower boats, as they are commonly called, aie particularly gay at New year time with flowers of all hues, and gaudy flues streaming from their mast and stern The crackers, or fireworks, of which the Chinaman is so fond, are let off in large quantities for several days in all parts of the town, and form part of their religious ceremonies or offerings to their gods.
